issues.item: Relationship Reminders: When people say things like my ex
issues.explanation: This trigger is hard to reconcile with the trauma type and the rest of the profile. For a 21-year-old married male relief worker in a war zone, military topics and Arabic shouting fit the reported trauma context, but 'my ex' is relationship-specific and not plausibly linked to the war-zone trauma as presented. It also does not connect well to the accompanying threat and memory items, which are clearly organized around combat/civilian danger cues rather than intimate-relationship themes.

vignette: Andreas's eyes would often glaze over when he recounted the events of that fateful day in the war-torn city where he had worked as a relief worker. He and his team had been distributing aid to civilians when a sudden explosion rocked the street, sending shrapnel flying everywhere. Andreas remembered seeing a young girl, no more than ten years old, lying motionless on the ground, her body torn apart by the blast. The image still haunted him, but what he couldn't shake off was the feeling of guilt that had settled in his chest like a stone. Why hadn't they been able to protect those people? Why hadn't they done more? As Andreas struggled to come to terms with what he had witnessed, he began to notice that certain things would trigger a visceral response in him. Whenever someone brought up military topics or talked about the war, he felt his anxiety spike. The sound of shouting in Arabic would send shivers down his spine, transporting him back to that chaotic scene. Even talking about the event itself became a minefield; Andreas couldn't bear to relive those moments without feeling like he was drowning in a sea of terror. To cope with these feelings, Andreas developed some maladaptive strategies. He started staying up late into the night, often until the early hours of the morning, hoping that exhaustion would dull his emotions. But even as he lay awake, he couldn't shake off the rumination that plagued him - thoughts about how things could have been done differently, how lives might have been saved if only they had acted sooner or more decisively. This preoccupation with prevention consumed him, making it hard for him to focus on anything else. Andreas also began avoiding situations that might bring him joy or hope. He stopped attending social gatherings with friends and family, fearing that their happiness would only serve as a cruel reminder of all he had lost. His wife, Rachel, noticed the change in him but struggled to understand why Andreas was pushing her away. She tried to reach out, to get him to talk about what was bothering him, but Andreas couldn't find the words. As time went on, Andreas's sense of threat began to seep into every aspect of his life. He felt uneasy around strangers, even in ordinary situations like grocery shopping or walking down the street. At night, he would wake up with a start, checking his surroundings to make sure he was safe. Sudden movements by others put him on high alert; he couldn't help but wonder if someone was lurking around the corner, waiting to strike. The memories of that day continued to haunt Andreas, feeling more like a current event than something relegated to the past. He would recall the terror he felt in vivid detail, reliving it as if no time had passed at all. The experience felt so extreme, so surreal, that sometimes Andreas questioned whether it had actually happened to him. It was this sense of disconnection from reality that finally brought Andreas to seek help. Rachel sat him down one evening and said, "Andreas, I don't know what's going on with you, but I do know that this isn't the man I married. You're disappearing before my eyes." Her words struck a chord; Andreas realized he needed to confront his demons head-on. Now, as he prepares for therapy, Andreas is most afraid of losing himself completely in the darkness of his memories. He hopes that by facing them, he can somehow find a way back to the person he once was - a person capable of experiencing joy and hope without being consumed by fear and guilt.
